name: Military–industrial complex
scope: The military-industrial complex is the critique, first given currency by Eisenhower's Farewell Address of 17 January 1961 (Britannica, s1; Eisenhower, s2), that the armed forces, their civilian departments in government, Congress and the arms industry form a self-interested alliance whose "unwarranted influence" can endanger liberties and democratic processes (Eisenhower, s2; Moyar, s6). This profile follows the American strand and its critical literature: Eisenhower's warning; the power-elite thesis of C. Wright Mills; the 1960s-70s critics collected in Pursell's reader (s3: Melman's Pentagon capitalism, Galbraith, Proxmire, Fulbright, Goodman, Lasswell's garrison state as forerunner), Suall's socialist version (s10) and Badger's thesis (s4); scholars note the term is both a neutral label for the defence sector and a pejorative for a dangerous special interest (Kieran and Martini and Roland, s8; Westbrook on Ledbetter, s5), and that its use for other countries is ambiguous. It excludes the general defence-industrial base as such, other "industrial complex" phrases (prison-industrial and similar), the Soviet and Russian cases, and the extreme-right movements Suall's pamphlet is mostly about.

sources.title: The Peace Race (Ballantine Books, 1961)
sources.author: Seymour Melman
sources.usedFor: Melman's book-length case against the arms race and for disarmament: independent unions and worker decision-making as checks on managerial power (ch. 5), disarmament and a strengthened UN (ch. 9-10), coexistence (ch. 13); also names the military-industrial complex and its lobbying (ch. 9).

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Melman's disarmament plan runs in stages to "total disarmament", with national forces reduced to police weapons and an international police force built up as armies shrink (The Peace Race, ch. 10, "International Cooperation for Dis-armament", and ch. 11); Eisenhower calls disarmament "a continuing imperative" (Farewell Address, section VI).

arbitrator-settles-disputes.rationale: In a disarmed world Melman would leave the "peaceful settlement of disputes" to strengthened UN bodies in place of military power (The Peace Race, ch. 10, "United Nations Organization for the Administration of Disarmament").

arms-reduction.rationale: Eisenhower calls disarmament "a continuing imperative" while keeping arms "mighty" for deterrence (Farewell Address, sections IV and VI); Melman objects to adding to American nuclear "overkill" (The Peace Race, ch. 13) and Goodman cites Marcus Raskin that "the real needs of our defense should cost less than a fourth of the budget" (Pursell ch. 23).

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Eisenhower warns against living for today at the expense of tomorrow, saying "we cannot mortgage the material assets of our grandchildren" and that democracy must not become "the insolvent phantom of tomorrow" (Farewell Address, section V); he does not name deficit stimulus itself.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Proxmire and Fulbright demand an end to the "blank check" issued to the military, and a 1969 congressional conference backed by them held that "Congressional control of military policy must be reasserted" (Pursell, introduction to Part IV, "Dimensions of the System").

conscription.rationale: Melman describes the draft as the one way of raising forces that also "guarantees decision-power by the military managers over a fixed proportion of the young people of the society", an extension of decision power "unprecedented in peacetime" (Pursell ch. 21, "Pentagon Capitalism", pp. 295-296).

corporate-influence.rationale: Eisenhower warns of "unwarranted influence" by the arms industry in "the councils of government" (Farewell Address, section III-IV), Proxmire reports that the complex's influence over the Pentagon has grown and calls the danger present (Pursell ch. 17, "Retired High-Ranking Military Officers"), Badger describes defence-industry lobbying of Congress (thesis ch. III, "Lobbying"), and Goodman calls the military-industrial firms "an overwhelming lobby" for the policies they profit from (Pursell ch. 23); these concern the arms industry, not business in general.

defeat-communism.rationale: Melman rejects the choice of "red or dead" and proposes to "win with freedom under peaceful coexistence", through a peace race and disarmament (The Peace Race, ch. 13, "How to Have Peaceful Coexistence - And Win").

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Melman says it "will certainly be necessary to strengthen the United Nations to enable it to keep the peace in a disarmed world and to enforce the rule of law", with a UN police force (The Peace Race, ch. 10).

experts-over-public.rationale: Eisenhower warns that "public policy could itself become the captive of a scientific-technological elite" and says "only an alert and knowledgeable citizenry can compel the proper meshing" of the military machinery with peaceful goals (Farewell Address, sections III-IV).

future-generations.rationale: Eisenhower says the nation must not live "only for today, plundering, for our own ease and convenience, the precious resources of tomorrow" and "cannot mortgage the material assets of our grandchildren" (Farewell Address, section V).

independent-unions.rationale: Melman holds that "the right of independent organization", from trade unions to poetry circles, is "an essential condition for freedom in modern industrial societies", and warns of a society in which "no independent organizations" are permitted (The Peace Race, ch. 5, "The Impotence of Conventional Politics").

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Mills holds that "the more trivial and glamorous aspects" of the national prestige system "distract attention from its more authoritarian features and to justify the power that it often conceals", and that celebrities can "distract the attention of the public" (The Power Elite, ch. 1, "The Higher Circles").

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: Melman condemns "a self-expanding war machine that uses military power for diverse political operations" and calls the Pentagon's operations abroad "parasitic" (Pursell ch. 21, closing paragraph); Bosch says the armed forces are sent abroad to win positions of power and arms profits at home (ch. 22, "Pentagonism").

military-superiority.rationale: Badger argues the United States must "be recognized as the superior military force in all types of warfare" (thesis ch. II, "Imperative Need") and Eisenhower wants arms "mighty, ready for instant action" (Farewell Address, section IV), while Melman and Goodman treat the arms race as futile and call for disarmament (The Peace Race, ch. 1 and 3; Pursell ch. 23).

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Melman proposes that disarmament free American capacity to "supply equipment and manpower on an abundant scale for the industrialization of the rest of the earth", "desirable on moral and political grounds" (The Peace Race, ch. 9, "Disarmament Without Depression"); Goodman names rescuing "the majority of mankind from deepening poverty" an indispensable international goal (Pursell ch. 23).

state-class-instrument.rationale: In The Power Elite, Mills coins 'power elite' to avoid 'ruling class' and says the American government is not, in any simple way, a committee of the ruling class; economic, political and military elites each hold some autonomy and decide through coalition.

unions-good.rationale: Melman writes that "the presence of autonomous trade unions in industry restrains the use of managerial position for dictatorial power" and that people "need organizations like trade unions to give them a voice" (The Peace Race, ch. 5).

workplace-democracy.rationale: Melman says worker decision-making "compels management to improve efficiency" and favours cooperatives, which "are democratic rather than managerial"; he says production goals can be "democratically decided with the participation of large numbers of people" (The Peace Race, ch. 5).

summary: The military-industrial complex is a warning, first made famous by Eisenhower in 1961, that the armed forces, the arms industry and their allies in government and Congress can build a self-serving power that threatens liberty and democratic control, and that only a watchful public can keep it in check. Later critics gave it different shapes: Mills's power elite, Melman's Pentagon capitalism (a state-run management that expands for its own sake and holds the nation's capital hostage), Galbraith's and Proxmire's call for closer civilian and congressional control, and Bosch's Pentagonism. The strand shares a concern with unaccountable defence spending and influence, and a wish to curb it; it has no single programme beyond that, and its defenders and critics disagree about how much military strength the country needs.

notes:
Searched every statement in the file against the Eisenhower address (s2), Pursell's reader (s3: Proxmire, Galbraith, Melman's Pentagon Capitalism, Bosch, Goodman, the editors' introductions), Badger's thesis (s4), Mills's The Power Elite (s11), Suall (s10) and Melman's The Peace Race (s13); most statements find no stated position and stay null. Positions on deterrence and nuclear weapons differ within the strand (Eisenhower and Badger want strong arms; Melman, Goodman and Bosch attack deterrence and the arms race, though Melman's unilateral-step criteria keep a second-strike capacity), so keep-nuclear-weapons and independent-nuclear-deterrent are left null: no source states them as asked; military-superiority is a split (0). Galbraith's chapter in s3 is on controlling the military through the civilian state and settles no statement; his books on price control, the 1929 crash and conservation, and the books on Imperial Japan, Georgia, Britain and technocrat art, were opened and are about other subjects, so none is cited. Suall (s10) is mostly about the extreme right and gives no stated position on any statement. Goodman is not a key figure and is cited only on arms and aid, where he repeats the critique; his decentralist and anti-growth views are not attributed to the strand. The unions and disarmament answers rest on Melman's Peace Race, a key figure's book on the subject. Aliases added: Pentagon system (Britannica) and Pentagonism and defense-space complex (Pursell, Nelson's essay).

Searched every statement against the saved sources (Eisenhower's farewell address, Britannica, Moyar, Mills's The Power Elite, the Pursell reader, Suall, Badger, Ledbetter review) and by web search on arms control, conversion, nationalisation of contractors (Galbraith, Melman), Pentagon secrecy and oversight (Fulbright), and Eisenhower's other speeches. The critique is a warning about one interest group's influence, not a programme; the reader's authors disagree with each other and propose single measures (nationalising munitions firms, conversion, disarmament) that do not settle the broader statements. Only the Mills statement on the state as a class instrument is settled; all others are null.
